text: A retailer routes 200,000 short customer messages a day into one of six queues. Routing must be fast and cheap, and the labels are simple. Which model and effort setting fit best?
options: A small, fast model such as Haiku, with effort set to low
The most capable model such as Opus at maximum effort, to avoid any misroutes
A mid-tier model at high effort, so it thinks carefully about every message
Whichever model has the largest context window, at its default effort
correct_answer: A small, fast model such as Haiku, with effort set to low
explanation: High-volume, simple classification fits a small, fast model at low effort (A). The chapter's exam trap is running the largest model at maximum effort on trivial classification (B), which multiplies cost and latency for no gain. High effort (C) spends extra thinking tokens on easy labels. Context window size (D) is irrelevant for short messages, and effort should be set explicitly, not left to a default.

text: A downstream system parses Claude's response as JSON. The prompt says "Respond only in valid JSON," but about 1 response in 200 still includes extra prose. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Repeat the JSON instruction in capital letters at the end of the prompt
Prefill the start of the assistant's reply with an opening brace
Pass a JSON schema in `output_config.format` so every response matches it
Extract the JSON from each response with a regular expression
correct_answer: Pass a JSON schema in `output_config.format` so every response matches it
explanation: Structured outputs (C) constrain the response so it always matches the schema; asking nicely is followed most of the time, not every time. Stronger wording (A) is still just a request. Prefilling the assistant's reply (B) is rejected with an error on current Claude models. Regular expressions (D) break on the first unusual answer. Remember that a schema guarantees shape only, so business rules are still checked in code.

text: A team enabled prompt caching on a 6,000-token system prompt, but `cache_read_input_tokens` is always 0. The system prompt begins with the line "Current time: " followed by the current timestamp. What is the fix?
options: Switch to the 1-hour cache lifetime so the cache does not expire between requests
Add three more `cache_control` breakpoints at different points inside the system prompt
Shorten the system prompt so it falls below the caching minimum
Move the timestamp after the last cache breakpoint, such as into the user message
correct_answer: Move the timestamp after the last cache breakpoint, such as into the user message
explanation: Caching needs an exact prefix match, so a timestamp at the top changes the prefix on every request and nothing is ever reused. Moving dynamic text after the last breakpoint (D) keeps the prefix stable. A longer lifetime (A) does not help when every prefix is different. More breakpoints (B) still sit after the changing timestamp. A prompt below the minimum length (C) is never cached at all.

text: A ticket classifier gives different labels to tickets that are almost identical, while its answers on hard tickets are fine. Which technique should you add first?
options: A few labeled examples that show the exact categories to use
A higher effort level so Claude reasons longer on every ticket
A larger model tier for all tickets, including the easy ones
A longer system prompt that describes every category in detail
correct_answer: A few labeled examples that show the exact categories to use
explanation: Diagnose before you add technique: inconsistent labels on similar inputs point to few-shot examples (A), which anchor the exact labels. More reasoning (B) and a larger model (C) target wrong answers on complex inputs, which is not the failure here. Longer abstract descriptions (D) help less than concrete examples when the problem is label consistency.

text: An agent follows 40 detailed procedures, but each request uses only one or two of them. All 40 are in the system prompt today. Which approach loads only what each request needs?
options: Enable prompt caching on the full system prompt and make no other changes to it
Package each procedure as a Skill that loads only when a request needs it
Truncate each procedure to its first paragraph to save tokens
Move all 40 procedures into the first user message of each request
correct_answer: Package each procedure as a Skill that loads only when a request needs it
explanation: Skills (B) use progressive disclosure: only the name and description are always present, and the full instructions load when a request needs them. Caching (A) makes the large prompt cheaper but still puts all 40 procedures in front of the model, so similar procedures still get mixed up. Truncating (C) removes detail the procedures need. Moving them into the user message (D) changes nothing about how much is loaded.
